Collagen is the primary structural component of all connective tissue. Bone, ligaments, and tendons are type I collagen, and cartulage is composed of type 2 collagen. Both types of collagen are formed from procollagen molecules, which consist of three protein strands in a triple helix formation. An enzyme produces active collagen, which alignes with other collagen molecules to form long filaments that are the components of microfibrils that form bundles as bone grows. The strength and durability of collagen sterm from strong cross-linking bonds, fomed between adjacent collagen bundles. the longitudinal grpuping of these bundles together forms ligaments and tendons. The bundles can also be arranged in layered sheets of varying directions, as found in fascia, bone, and cartilage.

Tendons are fibrous connective tissue connecting muscle to the periosteum of bone. Muscle contractions pull the tendon, causing the attatched bone to move. Ligaments are fibrous connective tissue connecting bone to bone. Ligaments contain elastin, a type of elastic protein that provide that provides the stretch needed for normal joint movement. Tendons and ligaments contain relatively few cells that require little oxygen and nutrients for metabolic activity. Because of the limited vasculature and circulation in tendons, regeneration after injury takes a significant amout of time and is sometimes not possiable without surgical intervention.

Minimal essential strain (MES) is the stimulus threshold required to initiate new bone growth. Catabolism is the process of breaking large molecules into smaller molecules to make energy aviable to the organism. Catabolism also can involv the breakdown of muscle tissue during periods of heavy training volume, low caloric intake, or high stress.

Essentoial physiological processes such as muscle growth and hormone balance rely on these reactions and continually occur so that the body can maintain homostasis. It is possible to evaluates an athlete's energy expenditure (metabolic rate) and fittness level using direct or indirect calorimetry.

ATP is a high-energy molecule used for muscle contractions, movement, and other life-sustaining metabolic process. ATP is an intermediate molecule (consisting of three primary parts- an adenine, a ribose, and three phosphates in a chain) that allows energy to transfer from exergonic to endergonic and catabolic to anabolic reaction. ATP is generated and replenished in skeletal muscle by three energy system: phosphagen, glucolytic, and oxidative.

Hydrolysis is a general term for any chemical reaction that breaks a chemical bond via the addition of whater. ATP hydrolysis plits ATP molecule into adenosione diphosphates (ADP) and usable energy. The enzyme adenosin triphosphatase (ATPase) is the catalyst fro the hydrolysis of ATP.

The phosphagen and glycolytic systems occur in the sacroplasm and are anaerobic mechanism, which means that they do not require oxygen. The eletron transport chain (ETC) and Kerbs cycle are aerobic mechanisms that require oxygen and occur in the mitochondria. The cellular respiration systems act in concert, rather than individually, to provide all required energy during exercise or rest.

title: CSCS Ch17: Program Design for Resistance Training

cards.a: Train for what you want to do. Training should mimic sport or be in line with goal when possible

cards.q: What does SAID stand for as it relates to resistance training?
cards.a: S - Specific A - Adaptation to I - Imposed D - Demands
Optimal adaptation occurs when training is done at the upper limit of the bodies ability

cards.q: What are some ways of inducing overload?
cards.a: 1) increasing load 2) increasing reps 3) increasing # of training sessions 4) adding exercises 5) adding sets 6) decreasing rest

cards.q: Wjat are the 7 key variable s (Steps) of progrsm desgin?
cards.a: 1) Needs Analysis 2) Exercise Selection 3) Training Frequency 4) Exercise Order 5) Training Load & Repititions 6) Volume 7) Rest

cards.q: What is involved on the first step (Needs Analysis) of program desgin?
cards.a: 2 stages: 1. Evaluate Sport/Goal - physiological/biomechanical profile - common injuries - position specific attributes 2. Athlete Profile - Look at training/injury status - testing

cards.q: How do you determine an individuals training status?
cards.a: 1) Determine injury status and history 2) Past training history/experiance - Type of program - length of training - Intensity - Exercise technique experiance 3) Physical testing - Body comp, flexilbility, strength, power, endurance, 1rm 4) Determine Goals - ex: strength, power, hypertrophy

cards.q: What is involved in the second step (exercise selection) of resistance training program desgin?
cards.a: Consider goals, exercise type, and past experiance
Exervises that recruit one or more large muscle areas. (Ex: chest, back, shoulders) - Involve 2 or more primary joints - Get priority during exercise selection
- Recruit small muscle groups (ex: calf, low back, upper arm) - Involve one primary joint - Secondary priority - More often used for injury prevention and rehab
- A sub classification of core exercises that involve loading of the spine, and muscular stabilization of posture
Structural exercises that are performed quickly or explosivly

cards.q: What should be kept in mind regarding athlete that play sports when desgining training programs?
cards.a: - Aim for sport specificity to increase transfer between training and sport
Exercises at the end of an session to promote recovery Light load resistance or low intensity aerobic activity Help to remove metebolic waste
A proper ratio of strength, power or musculat endurance of a muscle relative to another Not nessisarily meaning equal

cards.q: What should be considered in terms of equipment when desgining a program?
cards.a: Availability Ex: gym, home gym, bodyweight, dumbbells only

cards.q: How should available time per session factor into exercise selection?
cards.a: If limited time is available lower time exercises need to be given priority. Ex: machine leg press instead of barbbell lunges for hip quad training for a sprinter

cards.q: What factors should be considered in step 3 of resistance program desgin (training frequency)?
cards.a: 1) Training Status 2) Sport Season 3) Traing Load/type

cards.q: How often should and individual train based on training status?
cards.a: - Beginner = 2-3 - Intermediate = 3-4 - Advanced = 4-7

cards.q: What should the rest interval be between training days?
cards.a: - At least 1 day no more than 3 - As athletes become more advanced you can increase training days and decrease rest intervals up to 7 days a week of training using splits to rest muscle groups
- A method of increasing training frequency by dividing training into subsections of the body and resting after training by training an unrealted part Ex: Upper body, lower body split See pg 448

cards.q: What are resistance training frequency suggestions at diffrent point in a sport season?
cards.a: 1) Off season: 4-6 sessions/week 2) Preseason: 3-4 sessions/week 3) In-season: 1-3 sessions/week 4) Postseason: 0-3 sessions/week

cards.q: How does training load & tyoe effect trainibg frequency?
cards.a: - The greater the load (max/near max) the longer rest interval is needed to recover - Upper body recovers at a higher rate than lower body (reference 37) - Recovery is faster for single jpint exercises

cards.q: What other factors do you need to consider when determaining training frequency?
cards.a: - Other training (ex: sport skill) - Physically demanding jobs or other activities - both may reduced training frequencies and increase needed recovery

cards.q: What is the purpose of step 4 (exercise order) when developing resistance training protocols?
cards.a: Determine how to structure a session to maximize performance ability and adaptation from the session

cards.q: How should Power, other core & assistance exercises be ordered in a session?
cards.a: - Power exercises should be done first - Non power core exercises second - Assistance exercises last

cards.q: What cosiderations shluld be given to mentsl a physical fatigue regarding exercise order?
cards.a: - Higher technique exercises should be done first to avoid loss of form due to fatigue - larger》 smaller muscle groups

cards.q: What are the advanrages to alternating upper and lower body exercises within a session?
cards.a: - Rest one while training other - Good for begginers that find doing multiple exercises for same muscle group consecutively to hard - Can reduce session lengtg if time is a limiting factor

cards.q: What is the advantahe of an alternated push/pull session structure?
cards.a: - Alternating push and pull exercises ensure the same muscle group will not be used in 2 consecutive exercises thus maximizing recovery and thereby performance

cards.q: What is a superset & its advantages?
cards.a: - The preformance of 2 exercises consecutivly w/o rest that target opposing muscles - Increases training demand in time efficent manor
- The sequential performance without rest of 2 exercises that invole the same muscle group - Stress in compounded time efficently

cards.q: What is involved in step 5 (training load & repetitions) of resistance program desgin?
cards.a: - Determining: set, rep, load & rest schemes for optimal adaptations
The product of force and displacment. Important to quantify to avoid exahustion

cards.q: How is volume load or work in weight lifting terms calculated?
cards.a: Load x reps x sets
- 1RM is the max weight able to be use for one repitition - #RM is the max load able to be lifted for a predetermined # of reps

cards.q: What are the predicted reps attianable at 5% intervals of 1RM?
cards.a: 100% = 1 95% = 2 90% = 4 85% = 6 80% = 8 75% = 10 65% = 15 Accuracy of theses values is widely variable Can be used to predict 1RM from #RM Chart on pg 452

cards.q: What should be considered before doing a 1RM test?
cards.a: - should not be done with someone who is injured or medically supervised - experiance: shoukd only be done with intermidate or advance trained individuals- should not be done with someone who is injured or medically supervised - if a beginner 3RM may be a better choice because lack of technique and experiance increases risk of injury and deacreses accuracy of a 1RM test - if a beginner 3RM may be a better choice because lack of technique and experiance increases risk of injury and deacreses accuracy of a 1RM test

cards.q: Why are 3RM tests being suggested as a substitue for 1RM tests?
cards.a: - Reduced risk - Greater accuracy in begginers who lack proper technique

cards.q: What exercises should be used for 1RM tests?
cards.a: - Core exercises because they invole large muscle groups and multiple joints making them better able to deal with heavy loads - Chosen exercise should also have a stable easy to maintain form ex: fkat bench Poor Ex: bent over row, relies on postural muscles of the low back which can fatigue before 1RM is reached

cards.q: How should a 1RM test be preformed?
cards.a: 1) Warm up with a weight that allows 5-10 reps 2) Rest for 1 minute 3) Load a weight that individual can complete 3-5 reps with 4) Rest for 2 mins 5) Increase weight by 10-20lbs for upper body exercises or 30-40lbs for lower body exercises shoukd be able to complete 2-3 reps 5A) Might requier lower increases for less trained athletes 6) Rest 2-4 mins 7) Repeat increase 8) Attempt 1RM 9) If sucessful rest increase repeat 10) if failed rest decrease repeat

cards.q: How could to estimate 1RM for a true beginner?
cards.a: Use a 10RM test: - 10RM is not a good measure of power lower reps is preferable - Weight should be increase after warm up such that max is reached within 3-5 sets

cards.q: What % of 1RM should be used if the individuals goal is strength and for how many reps per set & how many sets?
cards.a: 85%, 6 reps or less for 2-6 sets

cards.q: What % of 1RM should be used if the individuals goal is power and for how many reps per set & how many sets?
cards.a: Single effort event: - 80-90%, 1-2 reps, 3-5 sets Multiple effort event: - 75-85%, 3-5 reps, 3-5 sets

cards.q: What % of 1RM should be used if the individuals goal is hypertrophy and for how many reps per set & how many sets?
What % of 1RM should be used if the individuals goal is muscular endurance and for how many reps per set & how many sets?
cards.a: No more than 67%, at least 12 reps, 2-3 sets

cards.q: Why is power trained at a lower weight then strength?
cards.a: Power is a distance over time measure therefore a measure of maximal load able to be moved at a high speed In contrast strength is simply define by the load one is able to lift without a time constraint therefore the movent is much slower but deals with higher loads

cards.q: How could a power or strength program be designed to combat the high physiological stress the body take during the high load training and avoid overtraining?
cards.a: - Program load variations into the weeks training sessions - Ex: have one day a week be the heavy day and 2 others be light and medium respectivly Monday: Heavy 85% 1RM Wednesday: light 80% load from Heavy day and preform same reps/sets even if able to do more Friday: medium 90% of heavy day same reps/sets

cards.q: What is the 2-for-2 rule for load progression?
cards.a: If an individaul can perform 2 more reps on their last set then perscribed for 2 workouts an increase is needed

cards.q: How much should load be increased by for good progression?
cards.a: Less trained/weaker: Upper body: 2.5-5lbs Lower body: 5-10lbs More trained/Stronger: Upper body: 5-10lbs Lower body: 10-15lbs OR 2.5-10% of current load

cards.a: Yes. Depending on the area of the body and the training goals, different loads can be assigned (75% of 1RM for upper body, 85% of 1RM for lower body) for different exercises affecting the different parts of the body. Different for Core and assistance exercises.

cards.q: What is the importance of determining an athlete's rep max (1RM or 10RM)?
cards.a: Knowing the 1RM or 10RM allows the trainer to assign proper training loads based off of a % of the RM. See table 15.7 on page 394

cards.q: What steps are involved when determining an athlete's rep max (1RM or 10RM)?
cards.a: A common strategy for testing is to conduct a 1RM test in several core exercises and use multiple-RM testing for assistance exercises.

cards.q: How is the rep max test chosen (1RM vs 10RM)?
cards.a: A common strategy for testing is to conduct a 1RM test in several core exercises and use multiple-RM testing for assistance exercises for sufficiently trained athletes. For untrained multiple-RM is needed instead of 1RM. 1RM should not be used for exercises that cannot provide valid and reliable data.

cards.q: How does the training load relate to the goal of training?
cards.a: Specific load and rep assignments via the RM continuum, a percentage of 1RM, or the results of multiple-RM testing can be applied to reach the training goal. Also the movement and physiological analysis of the sport and priorities of the sport season play a part. See table 15.9 page 401

cards.q: How does training load relate to training volume?
cards.a: Volume is based directly on the athlete's training goal. Usually the more volume the less load and vise versa. See table 15.11 page 406.

cards.q: How are intensities (HR, RPE) established for aerobic endurance training?
cards.a: The higher the intensity the shorter exercise duration. Monitoring O2 consumption during exercise to determine VO2max or measuring blood lactate are the best ways to establish proper intensity.

cards.q: How does the target HR change with different modes of aerobic training (long slow distance, interval training)?
cards.a: For LSD 80% of max HR so you will be in the THR zone a longer period of time (about 40 mins or so). Interval training is close to VO2max. See pages 498-499
It is the total amount of weight lifted in a training session.

cards.q: What are the different measures of training volume? How are they calculated?
cards.a: Rep-Volume is total number of reps in a session Load-Volume is total number of sets x reps x weight. Ex - 2 sets of 10 reps with 50 pounds = 1000 pounds.

cards.q: What activities or sports require training with high volumes? Low volumes?
cards.a: Strength less that 6 reps, 2-6 sets. Power single 1-2 reps, 3-5 sets. Power multi 3-5 reps, 3-5 sets. Hypertrophy 6-12 reps, 3-6 sets. Muscular endurance more that 12 reps, 2-3 sets

cards.q: How can training volume be manipulated to meet training goals (hypertrophy, etc)?
cards.a: Strength less that 6 reps, 2-6 sets. Power single 1-2 reps, 3-5 sets. Power multi 3-5 reps, 3-5 sets. Hypertrophy 6-12 reps, 3-6 sets. Muscular endurance more that 12 reps, 2-3 sets

cards.q: How does training volume relate to the goal of training?
cards.a: Volume is based directly on the athlete's training goal.

cards.q: How does volume relate to training status?
cards.a: For a beginner only 1-2 sets to start then add more sets as they progress until they reach the goals on table 15.11 page 406.

cards.q: How do the duration of the work and rest periods relate to the goal of training? To the involved energy systems?
cards.a: See table 2.7 on page 37. Phosphagen 5-10 secs of work; 1:12 to 1:20 ratio of rest. Fast Glycolysis 15-30 secs of work; 1:3 to 1:5 ratio of rest. Fast Glycolysis and Oxidative 1-3 mins of work; 1:3 to 1:4 ratio of rest. Oxidative greater 3 mins of work; 1:1 to 1:3 ratio of rest.

cards.q: How are the work:rest ratios assigned based on the goal of training? Of the involved energy systems?
cards.a: Strength 2-5 minutes of rest Power - Single and Multi event 2-5 minutes of rest Hypertrophy 30 seconds - 1.5 minutes of rest Muscular Endurance less than 30 seconds of rest

cards.q: What type of recovery method (passive or active) is recommended?
cards.a: Passive recovery especially after long duration and/or high intensity training sessions

cards.q: How does training frequency relate to the goal of training?
cards.a: It is the number of training sessions completed in a given time period, usually a week. The athlete's training status, sport season, projected exercise loads, types of exercises and other concurrent activities must be taken into account.

cards.q: How is frequency assigned based on the goal of training?
cards.a: Strength- 3 days a week, at least one but no more than 3 days of rest between. Plyometrics-2 to 4 a week, at least 48-72 hours of rest between. Aerobic-more than twice a week to increase VO2max but at least 1 day a week of rest.

cards.q: How does exercise progression relate to an athlete's current training status?
cards.a: The higher the athlete's condition or experience the more progression, however no more than 10% of the workload each week. Once higher levels of fitness are obtained only exercise intensity manipulation will allow progression.

cards.q: When and how (absolute or relative changes) should an athlete's training intensity, duration or frequency be increased?
cards.a: Depending on the season or the athlete's goal see table 18.5 pg 501. It is a relative change process. During off-season frequency is high, duration long, intensity is low to moderate. Preseason frequency very high, duration moderate to long, and intensity moderate to high. In-season frequency high, duration short, intensity low, Postseason frequency moderate, duration short, intensity low. This is an aerobic example.

cards.q: How does exercise progression relate to the goal of training?
cards.a: As an athlete adapts to training a strategy must be implemented for advancing exercise loads so the improvements will continue over time.

cards.q: What criteria should a strength and conditioning professional use to evaluate an athlete to determine proper exercise progression?
cards.a: Resistance is the 2 for 2 rule: perform 2 or more reps over last rep goal for a given exercise in the last two consecutive workouts, weight of 2.5-10% can be added. For aerobics heart rate, ratings of perceived exertion, METs or VO2max.

cards.q: What is periodization? What physiological responses are the basis of the periodization model?
cards.a: A preplanned, systematic variations in training specificity, intensity, and volume organized in periods or cycles within an overall program. The responses are from the GAS which is 3 phases: shock/alarm, resistance, exhaustion. Causes the body to be confused and to adapt to changes placed on it.

cards.q: What are the various periodization phases and what are they typical goals of each?
cards.a: Preparatory-base level of conditioning to increase tolerances to higher levels of training. First Transition-low intensity and volume for a week or so until the next phase. Competition-Very high intensity and low volume training and practicing in skill and game techniques. Second Transition-active rest and focuses on non-structured, non-sport activities, low intensity and volume.

cards.q: How do training volume and intensity change during the 4 sport season phases?
cards.a: Depending on the season or the athlete's goal see table 18.5 pg 501. It is a relative change process. During off-season frequency is high, duration long, intensity is low to moderate. Preseason frequency very high, duration moderate to long, and intensity moderate to high. In-season frequency high, duration short, intensity low, Postseason frequency moderate, duration short, intensity low. This is an aerobic example.

cards.q: How do these volume and intensity assignments vary based on a certain sport?
cards.a: See examples on page 385 etc.

cards.q: What is a needs analysis? How is it used to design a sport-specific training program?
cards.a: A 2-stage process that includes an evaluation of the requirements and characteristics of the sport and an assessment of the athlete. It is the first step in designing any exercise program.

cards.q: During what phase should sport-specific exercises be integrated into the periodization program?
cards.a: Competition Phase

cards.q: How do a sport's requirements help determine the training focus of a certain sport season?
cards.a: Through a needs analysis of the sport in question which include a movement, physiological, and injury analysis proper focus is placed on what is needed and how long each season should last depending on the nature of the sport and number of competitions.

cards.q: What is the training focus of an athlete just beginning a sport-specific training program?
cards.a: To establish a base line of condition to prepare them for more intense exercise routines and sport specific tasks.

cards.q: In what ways is an experienced athlete's training program different from a beginner's program?
cards.a: Advance athletes invariably train closer to their abilities and have smaller adaptational windows, their volume and intensity assignments are consistently higher.

cards.q: What forms of exercise are appropriate during the rehab process?
cards.a: Inflamation Phase-no exercise involving the injuried area Repair Phase-Isometric pain free exercises. Isokinetic and isotonic exercises can be used. Remodeling Phase-Functional training like joint-angle specific strengthening, velocity-specific, closed kinetic chain exercises, and exercises that enhance neuromuscular control.

cards.q: How can exercises be modified based on movement restrictions or contraindications caused by injury?
cards.a: Example of an athlete who needs to strengthen his upper body but has a shoulder injury in which a bench press may aggravate it. You would work in a different type of bench press (incline) or a different exercise altogether.

cards.q: If an area has been injured, what other body system (cardiovascular, muscular) must be addressed to maintain fitness level?
cards.a: Strategies to maintain cardiorespiratory fitness must be implemented during the inflammatory phase. Depending on the injury depends on the appropriate training program.
